tethers.statute: Immigration and Nationality Act — foreign-policy deportation ground
tethers.title: Deportable alien — foreign policy
tethers.enacted: 1952 (INA); the foreign-policy ground added by the Immigration Act of 1990
tethers.why: The provision the immigration judge found Sarsour removable under. It turns on the Secretary of State's determination of 'serious adverse foreign policy consequences', and its own text bars removal for lawful beliefs, statements or associations unless the Secretary personally finds a compelling foreign-policy interest — the exact line the appeal and the federal free-speech claim will test.

title: Signed Out
prompt: A judge says the U.S. can deport a Milwaukee mosque leader of 33 years on the Secretary of State's word. Is that the law protecting the country, or punishment for his speech?
framing: On Wednesday, September 30, 2026, Immigration Judge Jayme Salinardi of the Chicago Immigration Court ruled that the United States can deport Salah Sarsour, president of the Islamic Society of Milwaukee, Wisconsin's largest mosque. The judge found him removable on foreign-policy grounds, a rarely used provision that turns on the Secretary of State's judgment that a noncitizen's presence would have serious adverse consequences for U.S. foreign policy; Secretary Marco Rubio signed that determination. The judge threw out the government's claim that Sarsour lied on his green card application. Palestinian-born, Sarsour has lived in the U.S. since 1993 with no criminal record here; he was imprisoned in Israel in 1988 and convicted there in 1995, and says both confessions were coerced. ICE arrested him on March 30, 2026, and a federal judge ordered him released in June 2026. He has 30 days to appeal, and he cannot be deported while he does.

split.rationale: This is the rare clean axis. No station crosses zero at any band: A −0.5/−0.3/−0.8, C −0.7/−0.5/−0.9, B +0.4/+0.2/+0.7, D +0.6/+0.4/+0.9. What makes it more than a wall is the coalition band on both sides converging on the same move: argue the record (the 1988 and 1995 convictions, the statute's own carve-out for lawful speech) rather than the symbol. Both coalitions pull toward zero; both rims push away. Strength stays under 0.9 because the coalitions are close enough to talk (−0.3 and +0.2 at the institutional pair).

fluid.zReason: The statute's own speech carve-out requires a compelling foreign-policy interest beyond lawful speech, and the June district-court finding of a substantial targeting claim makes the appeal a likely place for the ground to fail.

The judge already tossed the green-card lie claim, and a federal judge in June called the targeting claim substantial. I'd expect the appeal to be where this comes apart.

The case is winnable on the law, and it'd be a shame to argue it on slogans.

The judge actually did the job carefully, throwing out the green-card fraud claim and ruling only on the ground that holds. The Israeli convictions weigh more with me than his speeches, and I expect the determination to survive appeal.

objectLayer.stated: A removability ruling on the foreign-policy ground: the Secretary of State judged that a lawful permanent resident's presence harms U.S. foreign policy, and the immigration court agreed.
objectLayer.operative: With the misrepresentation charge dismissed, removal rests on the Secretary's determination alone, under a provision whose text bars removal for lawful speech absent a personal finding of compelling interest. The operative question the appeal and the federal free-speech claim will test is whether the determination is about his Israeli convictions or his advocacy.
objectLayer.inversion: Lean, not ruled: no sign flip on the stated object. The object drifts from 'a security judgment' (stated) toward 'a speech case' (operative) — the left's centers read it there, and both right coalitions warn of the same drift from their side (B: 'a speech precedent won't stay pointed one way'; D: 'argue the convictions, not the speech').

blindAuthoring.authorNote: The z I trust least is B-coalition at +0.2: a rule-of-law conservative who fears the speech precedent could just as easily think the appeal succeeds, and I kept it positive only because deference to the Secretary on foreign affairs is the anchor for that station.
